reply.title: Why does a sigmoid squash any number into 0 to 1?
reply.story:
When building models that make binary decisions, scientists often need to turn any real-valued number into a probability between zero and one. If we simply truncate large values, the abrupt jumps create mathematical problems. Instead, we want a smooth transition that gently compresses the entire infinite number line into a finite interval.

Pierre François Verhulst faced a similar problem while studying how populations grow, leading him to develop the logistic curve. By scaling the input with a steepness parameter and shifting it by a midpoint, the function creates an S-shaped curve that approaches zero as the input drops and one as the input rises.

At the heart of this behavior is the exponential function in the denominator. As the input grows very large, the exponential term vanishes, leaving one over one. As the input drops far below zero, the exponential term dominates, pushing the fraction down to zero. The derivative gives us the slope, showing how sensitive the transition is at any given point.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how the logistic sigmoid maps any real number into the interval from $0$ to $1$. Adjust the steepness, midpoint, and marker to examine the curve and its slope.
